question: Under only smoothness, small-step, finite-precision, and random-initialization assumptions, what execution patterns force shuffled mini-batch SGD to fit its training set, and how much fresh randomness can perturbed full-batch gradient descent need to escape hard local behavior?

key_findings.claim: A sufficiently small gradient step on a known batch is injective, so an SGD trajectory can be reconstructed backward from its final weights and batch order.
key_findings.evidence: For an L-smooth batch loss and step size below 1/L, equality of two post-update parameter vectors would imply a strict norm contraction unless their pre-update vectors are equal. The finite-precision formulation retains this injectivity, although reconstruction enumerates the entire parameter grid.

key_findings.claim: The paper converts a batch-versus-history accuracy gap into compression of the random permutation used by SGD.
key_findings.evidence: Its accuracy discrepancy sums Bernoulli KL divergences between accuracy on previously seen examples and accuracy on the immediately preceding batch. A set-encoding lemma makes each large divergence save about b times that divergence in the description of the epoch's batches.

key_findings.claim: Persistently high accuracy discrepancy is a sufficient condition for perfect training accuracy in a constant number of epochs.
key_findings.evidence: Incompressibility of random epoch permutations upper-bounds average discrepancy while the stopping condition has not fired. Corollary 3.3 reverses this argument: if every epoch exceeds the global threshold plus a margin, continued execution would compress an incompressible random string, so SGD must terminate with 100% training accuracy.

key_findings.claim: Sublinear perturbation randomness cannot uniformly make full-batch gradient descent solve every smooth classification instance in polynomial time, even with many parameters.
key_findings.evidence: The proof embeds a perturbed-GD subroutine in a shuffled-batch procedure on random labels. If each batch could be fit with only o(m) random bits and polynomial work, batch accuracy would create enough discrepancy to force impossible nontrivial whole-dataset accuracy; Theorem 4.3 therefore supplies a hard instance requiring exponential work.

key_findings.claim: The MNIST experiment is a qualitative consistency check, not an empirical test of either main convergence or randomness theorem.
key_findings.evidence: The experiment uses one-hidden-layer GELU networks, three widths, three batch sizes, one learning rate, and 300 epochs. It reports that discrepancy scales roughly inversely with squared batch size and decays for weak models, but does not estimate the theorem's hidden threshold, test O(1)-epoch termination, or measure random-bit requirements.

key_findings.claim: The advertised minimality is mathematical rather than operational: the sufficient statistic can be as expensive to evaluate as full-dataset training accuracy, and the proof's decoder need not run efficiently.
key_findings.evidence: Accuracy discrepancy repeatedly evaluates parameters on growing subsets of the data, while Theorem 2.2 reconstructs a predecessor by exhaustive enumeration over the finite parameter space. Kolmogorov description length permits that computation, but it does not provide a practical monitor or algorithm.

method.core_idea: Treat the random data permutations consumed by SGD as incompressible strings and prove that a long, high-discrepancy execution would encode those strings too concisely.
method.mechanism: Use small-step reversibility to reconstruct weights backward, encode each batch from the smaller set of examples it classifies like the batch, quantify the saving with Bernoulli KL divergence, and contradict the Kolmogorov complexity of random permutations. Reuse that accounting in a reduction that lower-bounds the random bits needed by a perturbed-GD subroutine.
assumptions: Every per-example loss is differentiable and L-smooth on a finite-precision parameter grid.
The gradient step is smaller than 1/L and the approximate finite-precision gradients preserve L-smoothness.
Each epoch uses an independent uniformly random permutation of the training set.
The analysis concerns training accuracy only and uses an explicit termination test on the entire data set.
The perturbation family in the lower bound is reversible and is represented with a number of random bits proportional to its dimension.
Kolmogorov decoders may use unbounded computation; only their program length is charged.

techniques.role: Turns a hypothetical long randomized execution into an overly short description of its random choices.
Measures batch-local progress relative to the model's accuracy on earlier examples through Bernoulli KL divergence.
Makes the final weights and encoded batches sufficient to reconstruct earlier SGD states.
Converts a universally successful low-randomness perturbation routine into an impossible under-capacity classifier.

evaluations.setting: MNIST and MNIST with independently randomized labels; one-hidden-layer GELU networks of width 2, 5, or 10; batch sizes 50, 100, or 200; 300 epochs.
evaluations.metric: Epoch-averaged accuracy discrepancy and training accuracy.
evaluations.result: Discrepancy is reported to have an inverse-squared batch-size scale; on randomized labels it trends below an apparent capacity-insensitive level, and it behaves similarly for small models on ordinary MNIST.
evaluations.baseline: The same SGD configuration across three widths and three batch sizes; no competing optimizer or theorem-derived numerical threshold.

limitations: Author-stated: the work does not study generalization; every accuracy quantity concerns the training set.
Author-stated: the theory covers vanilla shuffled mini-batch SGD without momentum, regularization, acceleration, or common data-augmentation behavior.
Reviewer inference: the universal discrepancy threshold is hidden in asymptotic notation and is not computed, so the sufficient condition is not directly testable on a run.
Reviewer inference: evaluating discrepancy needs repeated predictions over large historical subsets and can erase the diagnostic's practical value.
Reviewer inference: exhaustive reverse reconstruction establishes description-length existence rather than an efficient decoder.
Reviewer inference: the perturbation theorem proves a worst-case hard instance and does not characterize the random bits actually needed on neural-network benchmarks.
Reviewer inference: three tiny MNIST widths and no reported seed variation are too narrow to support claims about modern overparameterized training.
failure_modes: A step size at or above the injectivity bound makes the backward reconstruction argument fail.
Momentum, optimizer state, data augmentation, replacement sampling, or nondeterministic kernels add unencoded state and invalidate the stated decoder.
Training loss can improve while 0-1 accuracy discrepancy remains small or discontinuous, making the condition silent.
A model that cannot reach exactly 100% accuracy never triggers the paper's primary stopping condition, even if it reaches a useful solution.
An unknown large constant in the global threshold can make the asymptotic sufficient condition vacuous at practical data sizes.
Non-reversible or adaptively generated perturbations lie outside the random-bit lower-bound formulation.
reusable_insights: Randomness accounting can reveal impossible optimizer traces without assuming a specific neural architecture.
A local-progress diagnostic should be separated into statistical sufficiency, online measurability, and computational cost.
Reversible training updates can support forensic reconstruction and information-budget arguments even when they are not computationally invertible in practice.
Worst-case randomness lower bounds should report the entropy source, precision model, and whether randomness is one-shot or refreshed during optimization.
open_questions: Can the hidden discrepancy threshold be made explicit and nonvacuous for finite data sets?
Is there a cheaply estimable proxy for accuracy discrepancy with finite-sample confidence bounds?
Can the compression proof cover momentum, replacement sampling, augmentation, and adaptive learning rates by encoding their additional state?
Does any version of the argument predict grokking time or delayed generalization, rather than only exact training fit?
What is the sharp random-bit complexity of escaping strict saddles under bounded dimension, precision, and oracle access?
Can the hard perturbation instance be made natural enough to distinguish practical optimizers?

competitive_landscape.title: Neural Network Weights Do Not Converge to Stationary Points: An Invariant Measure Perspective
competitive_landscape.difference: Zhang et al. explain stable loss without stationary parameters through approximate invariant measures and large-scale experiments; this paper instead derives a training-accuracy sufficient condition from compressibility of shuffled batch orders.

competitive_landscape.title: An Alternative View: When Does SGD Escape Local Minima?
competitive_landscape.difference: Kleinberg et al. obtain escape behavior when neighborhood-averaged gradients satisfy one-point convexity and relate noise scale to smoothing; this paper removes that geometric condition but gives an execution-pattern implication rather than an optimizer-wide convergence guarantee.

competitive_landscape.title: How to Escape Saddle Points Efficiently
competitive_landscape.difference: Jin et al. give a constructive perturbed-gradient algorithm reaching second-order stationary points in nearly dimension-free polynomial time under smoothness conditions; this paper asks how many random bits any reversible perturbation family needs in a worst case.

competitive_landscape.title: Gradient Descent Can Take Exponential Time to Escape Saddle Points
competitive_landscape.difference: Du et al. construct natural saddle chains that slow randomly initialized unperturbed GD exponentially; this paper's reduction instead lower-bounds perturbation entropy for uniform success over smooth classification instances.

competitive_landscape.title: Limitations of SGD for Multi-Index Models Beyond Statistical Queries
competitive_landscape.difference: Barzilai and Shamir develop a non-statistical-query framework for limitations of actual vanilla SGD on structured single- and multi-index targets; the reviewed paper is architecture-agnostic but its impossibility is mediated by a low-randomness perturbed-GD subroutine and random labels.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: Entropy compression yields a model-agnostic accuracy-discrepancy condition for constant-epoch perfect fitting and a linear random-bit lower bound for perturbed GD on some smooth instances.
novelty_assessment.evidence: Sections 3 and 4 construct two explicit incompressibility contradictions from reversible gradient steps and shuffled batches.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The distinctive contribution is the information-theoretic encoding of SGD's data-order randomness and its reuse in a perturbation lower bound. It does not replace geometric convergence or saddle-escape theory: the threshold is asymptotic, monitoring is expensive, the decoder is computationally unbounded, and the experiment verifies only two qualitative scaling patterns. The author's arXiv:2111.05478 is an earlier same-title lineage with materially different local-progress and simplicity assumptions, not an independent competitor.
